articles.title_orig: Unprecedented Collab Between China and the Met Uncovers Secrets of Chinese Mural During Exhaustive Reproduction
articles.title_zh: Unprecedented Collab Between China and the Met Uncovers Secrets of Chinese Mural During Exhaustive Reproduction
articles.content_orig:
A major arts and heritage conservation project in China has born unexpected fruit thousands of miles away in New York City.
In the Chinese arts and antiquities gallery of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a 50-foot-long mural devours the attention of an entire room with its arrangement of Buddha and his attendants.
The Medicine Buddha mural had long attracted the wonder of Zhang Jian, director of the “Meticulous Painting Institute” at the Chinese National Academy of Arts, which since 2013 has poured billions of Chinese RMB into restoring, conserving, and repatriating Chinese artifacts around the country and the world.
Describing it as wielding an “awe-inspiring energy,” Zhang learned that the mural was originally located in the ancient Guangsheng Temple in central China. Standing in its halls years later, staring at the vacant space where the massive mural had originally hung, Zhang was struck with an idea.
Over the next 3 years, he led a team of special artists and conservationists to the Met to meticulously—excruciatingly—copy the mural for a life-sized replica that captures every single crack, faded contour, and conservationist correction it had faced in its 700 years on the Earth.
This project was made possible with the unerring support of the Met itself, a collaboration which marks arguably the highest ever undertaken between Chinese and American cultural institutes.
Now in October, the Met is to co-host an international symposium in Beijing about Chinese murals, marking the first time the New York museum has jointly held a major academic conference in China with a national research body.
Jason Sun, the Met’s curator of Chinese art, told the South China Morning Post that the results achieved by Zhang’s team—including the realization that conservators had incorrectly arranged the mural segments so that Lord Buddha’s head was 2 centimeters off kilter—as having “profound historical and practical significance.”
Painted around 700 years ago during the Mongol-administered Yuan Dynasty, on clay tiles mixed with rice straw, the mural depicts the Medicine Buddha seated with his chief attendants surrounded by numerous figures.
Yet its presence in the Met isn’t the result of it being a plundered relic. Mainland China was mostly free from Western colonial occupation when the impoverished monks from Guangsheng Temple chopped the mural up into sections and sold it to fix the collapsing roof of their temple.
Among the keystones of Buddha’s teachings is the unavoidable truth that all things are impermanent, so if they were good students of the Great Sage, those impoverished monks would not have hesitated to part with the relic, that traded hands across the West until it arrived at the Met via donation from Arthur Sackler in 1965.
The China National Arts Fund, a state-endowed philanthropic fund established in 2013 under the National Academy of Arts, was as recently as 2025 tasked specifically with the preservation of ancient murals and other works. So far, 40 ancient murals from caves and temples across Western China have been painstakingly examined and copied, but if they are held overseas, the Fund has the directive to pay for their study, and potentially, their recreation.
Yet Zhang had a different sort of intention for that recreation: one that the Met administrators enthusiastically supported. In 2024, SCMP reports that the Fund had formalized a research partnership with the Met, whereby the famous museum granted their colleagues in East Asia full authorization for prolonged detailed study of the work, and the sharing of ultra-high-resolution digital images.
CHINESE MURALS IN THE NEWS: Stunning Tang Dynasty Mural Unearthed in China Portrays a ‘Westerner’ with Blonde Hair
“The Met staff actively coordinated with visitors for us,” said Meng Ying, an artist on Zhang’s team which visited the Met 3 times over the following years. “Though our lifts and lighting equipment occasionally blocked sightlines, visitors were remarkably understanding.”
As Meng said, studying portions of the work required specialized hydraulic lifts and expansive light fixtures, conditions which he described as being “unprecedented” in the history of the Met. This went on for days at a time, while the team poured their attention onto the smallest details to reproduce exactly what it was that the Guangsheng Temple was missing.
This included using clay-rich mud and rice straw to make the tiles, which they sourced from as close to the temple as possible. It involved extensive studying into the mineral pigments—considering what would have been available to the medieval painters, and how such materials could have changed over 700 years.
“Lighting, digital cameras ,and printing all change how a color looks. We had to tweak our paints over and over again on site,” said Han Maoyuan, another artist on the team.
MORE COLLABORATION LIKE THIS: Since 1968 French Teachers Have Come to Louisiana Classrooms to Preserve French Language Through Immersion
Yet further, the team layered their mud tiles to create a base-layer painting and a second to replicate the scars left by time and intervention.
As mentioned earlier, the team’s exhaustive examination of the mural revealed that its original mounters in the Met’s galleries had misunderstood Chinese brushwork, and misaligned the Buddha’s head by 2 centimeters. Met staff told SCMP that after the disbelief wore off, they couldn’t walk through the room without noticing that the Buddha’s head was crooked.
The finished mural produced by Zhang and his team made its public debut at the China National Arts and Crafts Museum in Beijing, where on September 24th, in honor of President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US, an exhibition was held featuring the fruits of the National Art Fund’s preservation and reproduction efforts.
FROM THE MET: Rare Chinese ‘Magic Mirror’ That Projects Hidden Image Rediscovered After Decades in Museum Storage
Zhang said it would allow this ancient mural to re-enter contemporary cultural life, yet with all the context that great works of art carry with them as the centuries load up on their shoulders.
Other murals from Guangsheng, as it turns out, are located in American Museums—in Cincinnati and Missouri—both have which have already contacted Zhang for the purpose of examining the alignments and conditions of the works.

articles.title_orig: The RTX 5090 Isn’t ‘Alive’ if It Costs $10,000, No Matter What Nvidia Says
articles.title_zh: The RTX 5090 Isn’t ‘Alive’ if It Costs $10,000, No Matter What Nvidia Says
articles.content_orig:
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn't affect our editorial independence .
I’ve been buying Nvidia graphics cards exclusively for nearly 30 years, and I may well continue—if Nvidia will let me. But even I’ve had to make peace with the fact that Nvidia is no longer in the business of supporting PC gaming. I’m not sure it ever will be again.
I was thinking about this while listening to the latest episode of The Full Nerd, in which Adam and his fellow cohosts discuss what it means that Nvidia may soon stop selling the RTX 5090 entirely. The news comes courtesy of a Twitter (sorry, X ) post from a known leaker with a decent track record, so while you should take it with a grain of salt it seems like there’s a strong possibility it will prove true.
Welcome to The Full Nerd newsletter—your weekly dose of hardware talk from the enthusiasts at PCWorld. Missed the surprising topics on our YouTube show or the latest news from across the web? You’re in the right place.
Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website !
And honestly, it doesn’t seem that surprising when you consider that the RTX 5090 launched with an MSRP of $1,999 yet regularly sold for upwards of $5,000, due in no small part to massive demand from AI-pilled coders and companies looking to take advantage of that sweet, sweet 32GB of DDR7 memory. A casual search of the major retailers this week turned up precisely zero 5090 cards available for purchase, even at that exorbitant price, and I suspect that will remain true for the foreseeable future.
It can feel heartbreaking if you’re dedicated to the hardcore DIY PC gaming lifestyle, but you can take solace in the fact that the GeForce RTX 5080, RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5070 are still widely available and plenty good enough for high-res, high-speed PC gaming. Heck, the same leak that suggests the RTX 5090 is done for also claims that Nvidia will launch a new model of RTX 5080 with 24GB of DDR7 memory, which should offer a noticeable improvement over the current 16GB RTX 5080 cards.
But I have to say, the sooner you make peace with the fact that Nvidia is no longer in the business of supporting PC gaming, the better. Don’t get me wrong, Nvidia will continue to make new desktop graphics cards and talk a big game about how it values PC game players first and foremost. But the numbers have shown otherwise for some time, and that’s likely to continue for years to come.
After all, the AI-driven explosion of demand for high-end GPUs and silicon helped Nvidia become the first trillion-dollar chip company , and recent financial reports and SEC filings show the company’s revenue from data center products is now 4-5x that of its consumer hardware revenue. That’s presumably part of the reason why the company recently stopped reporting GPU sales as a discrete category entirely, instead lumping all GPU hardware sales (for both commercial and retail customers) into one category on its balance sheet alongside robotics, automotive and telecom products.
So please, for your own mental health, I’m begging you: do not give in to Jensen’s sales pitches at the next Nvidia press conference. I believe the company will keep making new graphics cards for the foreseeable future, but only to hold on to its commanding hold of the GPU market and keep up appearances while it milks the AI boom for all its worth. If AI demand collapses the way crypto seemed to crash a few years ago, maybe we’ll see Nvidia take up the mantle of being a PC gaming company once again.
But I don’t expect that will happen any time soon, and making peace with that has done wonders for the stress I feel right now as a frustrated fan of PC gaming. It’s helped me realize that I don’t need the latest and greatest hardware to have a blast gaming on my PC, and the same can be true for you. Take this time to play some games in your Steam(ing) pile of shame, get deeper into Linux gaming and explore all the other cool things you can do without an RTX 5090. Because I don’t know that high-end GPUs will be affordable for regular folks like you and me in the next few years, if ever—and I don’t think I’ll be buying an Nvidia GPU any time in the near future.
This week your regular host Adam Patrick Murray was joined by PCWorld’s Brad Chacos and Michael Crider on episode 419 of The Full Nerd to chat about the rumored end of the GeForce RTX 5090, open-source Adobe Creative Cloud alternatives and the pending launch of RTX Spark laptops.
And of course, the trio also make time to answer your questions from the PCWorld Discord and the live chat about everything from the future of PC game streaming to the durability of flash drives. Make sure to check it out, and tune in to next week’s episode to get your questions answered on the air!
From some fun new ideas about where to place your GPU to an elucidating new interview that reveals the PC gaming habits of one of Hollywood’s movers and shakers, here’s some fun nerd news I found around the web for you this week!
That’s it for your Full Nerd newsletter this week! Until next week, be sure to bookmark PCWorld and keep an eye on the YouTube channel for our latest videos straight out of the PCWorld studio. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website !

Alex Wawro has more than 15 years experience as a tech journalist, and has covered everything from laptops and CPUs to PC gaming and handhelds. As part of PCWorld's video team, you can see him going hands-on with the latest and greatest tech on YouTube, TikTok, and Reels, and his writing will appear on PCWorld.com. articles.title_orig: Finland gripped by national broadcaster’s puppies live stream
articles.title_zh: Finland gripped by national broadcaster’s puppies live stream
articles.content_orig:
Yle’s 24-hour puppy livestream has become a popular distraction as Finland heads into its long, dark winter.
Yle’s “Pentulive” – Finnish for “Puppy Live” – follows Hilkka, a Lagotto Romagnolo, and her new litter as they sleep, play and suckle. The broadcaster says the stream has drawn millions of viewers to its website.
Hilkka gave birth to two female and four male puppies on October 10. The webcam went live shortly afterward, and the puppies are expected to remain on screen until they leave for their new homes in December.
Because puppies need up to 20 hours of sleep a day, there can be little action. Now in its sixth season, “Pentulive” has been called “slow TV,” a format first tried in Norway in 2009, when the Norwegian public broadcaster aired a seven-hour train journey.
A Yle press statement says viewers can watch the puppies reach milestones, including opening their eyes, learning to walk and playing outside for the first time. The breeder is anonymous.
Finland has just under 5.66 million residents, but Yle says the “Pentulive” page recorded 6.5 million views last year, while its social media channels drew 20 million views. Based on viewing figures so far, this year’s litter appears set to attract even more viewers.
Finland is among the world’s northernmost countries and is preparing for its long, dark winter. Temperatures can fall to -50°C (-58°F), and in parts of the country north of the Arctic Circle the sun stays below the horizon for weeks. The livestream offers residents a cozy diversion from the cold and darkness.
Yle science reporter Pirjo Koskinen launched the puppy-cam in 2021 as part of a series on canine science. She told CNN by email that one aim was “to shed light on a dog’s crucial first few weeks,” adding: “What happens at the breeder’s – much like with human children – influences the rest of the dog’s life.”
Koskinen said the stream’s appeal also lies in offering a break from daily life: “It is all about caring, love, and nurturing – all those positive aspects of humanity that often get pushed aside by a constant stream of unpleasant news,” she said. “‘Puppy Live’ offers comfort and relaxation amidst the rush of everyday life; it’s a wonderful escape from the human world into a ‘puppy bubble.’”
Sonja Mutanen, a doctoral researcher studying media and animals at the University of Eastern Finland, said the streams are a much-anticipated feature of the dark winter months for many Finns. “This kind of feel-good content can foster a sense of belonging and emotional well-being, which is important during late autumn and winter when people tend to stay at home more,” she told CNN.
Miiamaaria Kujala, an adjunct professor of comparative cognitive neuroscience at the University of Helsinki, told CNN by email that a live feed affects viewers differently from the short videos common on social media. “The live stream offers something that appears to be missing from many of the modern busy lives: something real, genuine and fragile,” she said. “Pentulive is life-paced: It contains very calm periods and unexpectable action periods. As a live feed, it likely provokes more intense emotional responses from the observers … but it is also immensely calming to observe a sleeping puppy.”
The stream also creates a “sense of continuity as it follows the puppies growing older,” Kujala said. “They’re not just random animals, you learn to know them individually.”
This is the second litter for 5-year-old Hilkka, who is currently on leave from her work as a “school dog,” providing emotional support to pupils.
The breeder has given the puppies nicknames, but they are due to receive official names on Saturday. Viewers will narrow down the options, and the puppies will “choose” among them by sitting in a circle of sealed envelopes and sniffing at the one they like.

articles.title_orig: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.title_zh: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive / Saudi postpones FII in person after Wall Street lobbying
articles.title_zh: Exclusive / Saudi postpones FII in person after Wall Street lobbying
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks.
The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29. "We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon," the conference organizers said in a statement .
The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured.
Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference. They included JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs' David Solomon, Blackstone's Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock's Larry Fink and Citigroup's Jane Fraser.
CNBC was told some participants and speakers had planned to travel to Saudi Arabia by flying first to Bahrain and then driving five hours to Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund launched the Future Investment Initiative in 2017. The conference  has played a key part in Riyadh's plans to diversify its oil-dependent economy. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveiled the ambitious megaproject NEOM at the first conference in 2017.
The decision to postpone the conference underscores the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East as the U.S-Iran war spreads across the region. Houthi militants have launched repeated waves of missile and drone strikes at Saudi Arabia since the deadly airport attack earlier this month.
The Houthis claimed on Monday to have attacked King Khalid International Airport again; Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia, close to Yemen; Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea Coast; the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi naval forces.
The Saudi military destroyed several drones launched at the Riyadh region on Friday and Saturday, a spokesperson for the kingdom's armed forces said. Missiles launched over the Red Sea were also intercepted Friday including one heading toward the port city and oil terminal Yanbu, the spokesperson said.

Russian forces have launched a large-scale combined attack on Kyiv Oblast using attack drones, ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, killing one person and injuring 10. Three people remain missing.
Source: Tymur Tkachenko, Head of Kyiv Oblast Military Administration, on Telegram ; State Emergency Service (SES) of Ukraine
Quote from Tkachenko: "Six people have been injured in Irpin, Bucha district, including three children. Another three people are missing. Search operations are currently underway."
Details: Tkachenko added that 11 houses, six cars, industrial and warehouse premises and an educational institution were damaged in the Bucha district. Windows were shattered in apartment buildings.
In the Vyshhorod district, a house, five cars and an infrastructure facility were damaged.
Update: The SES later added that one person had been killed and 10, including three children, had been injured as a result of the Russian attack.
Quote from SES: "Three more people remain missing. The information about people killed and injured is constantly updating."
The SES added that firefighters had contained the fire on the warehouse premises and efforts to extinguish it were ongoing.

articles.title_orig: Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov, 51, OBM
articles.title_zh: Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov, 51, OBM
articles.content_orig:
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a longtime educator and respected member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday morning. Full Story
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a longtime educator and respected member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday morning. Full Story
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a beloved educator and longtime member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday, 8 Cheshvan, 5787.
Rabbi Malov suffered a sudden cardiac arrest shortly after waking up and washing Negel Vasser. Emergency responders were called to his home but were unable to revive him.
His sudden passing has shocked the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad and his many friends and acquaintances throughout Israel and around the world.
Rabbi Malov served as the Rebbe’s Shliach in Kfar HaRif and dedicated much of his life to Jewish education. For many years, he directed the neighborhood’s evening yeshiva program, where hundreds of children gathered nightly in the local shul to study Torah.
Friends described him as a devoted educator and accomplished Torah scholar, knowledgeable in both Nigleh and Chassidus, who worked tirelessly to spread Torah learning.
He also organized annual Kinusei Torah in the neighborhood around Yom Tov, in accordance with the Rebbe’s directive to hold Torah gatherings during the holidays.
Rabbi Malov was the son-in-law of Rabbi Yitzchak Yehuda Yeruslavsky , Rov of Nachlas Har Chabad and a leading Chabad Rov.
He was born in Bnei Brak to Rabbi Tzvi Eliyahu Malov , OBM, a longtime Chabad communal activist in Yerushalayim who passed away approximately six years ago, and Mrs. Chana Chaya Malov , daughter of R’ Yaakov Moshe Hakohen Halperin , who passed away in Tishrei 5751 at the age of 40.
He is survived by his wife, Mrs. Nechama Dina Malov , and their children: Menachem Mendel, Shterna Sarah Kramer, Devorah Leah , and Mushka .
The levaya will depart from his home in Nachlas Har Chabad at 12:30 PM, passing the local Talmud Torah and central shul before proceeding to Shamgar in Yerushalayim.
The levaya will depart Shamgar at 3:00 PM for burial at Har Hamenuchos in Yerushalayim.

The move comes after the California-based company revealed 25 new spots were coming across 14 states.
Some recent openings include West Palm Beach, Fla., on June 12, the New Orleans, La., location on June 10 and the Tucson, Ariz., location on May 29.
As of Oct. 12, the fan-favorite grocery chain revealed it will open the following:
Trader Joe’s did not set an opening date for the new locations, but it did tell Nexstar that locations marked as “opening soon” typically open three to six months after announcing them online.
The newest spot open to the public is in Reading, MA, as shoppers could start browsing aisles on Oct. 14.

articles.title_orig: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.title_zh: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.content_orig:
Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.
The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.
Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.
But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.
Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.
In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.
It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.
The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.
Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.
He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.
Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.
While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.
Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.
In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.
"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.
It is still not known when he might return to Spain.
Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.
The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.
The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.
But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.
The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.
But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.
And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

A Chinese-speaking hacker has been observed using artificial intelligence (AI) agents to probe and then gain unauthorized access to more than 100 websites belonging to some extremely well-known companies. From Deere, the farming equipment manufacturer, to SharkNinja, the company behind beloved kitchen appliances, the agents were able to leverage exposed instances of Carin, an open-source AI-powered problem-solving platform that has proven popular among hackers, a Reuters report explains.
This is just the latest example of hackers turning to AI agents in an attempt to level up their attacks on unsuspecting companies and services. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge, spotted the hacker's antics when observing Carin instances that had been inadvertently exposed.
Fagerland was able to watch multiple hackers go about their business, but the Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific, the report says. They targeted businesses based in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japanese e-commerce sites. Notably, the hacker didn't get into detail when commanding their legion of AI agents. Fewer than 100 Chinese characters were used, yet the agents had attempted ot break into more than 1,200 different websites as of the week ending October 18, 2026.
These agents weren't simply throwing everything at a wall and hoping it stuck, either. Security researcher Fagerland was "impressed" by some of the tactics that had been used. In one case, the AI agents scoured digital records to find infrastructure associated with their target, located a public-facing control panel, identified a weakness, and then leveraged it to force the execution of malicious commands, the Reuters report detailed. "It's ⁠not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland told Reuters . "It's not script kiddie stuff."
Vitally, the approach of using AI agents in this way means that they can be given instructions and then left to their own devices. With no supervision required, those commanding the agents are free to turn their attention elsewhere. While SharkNinja told Reuters that the attack only impacted a site used for product support information, the rest of the AI-aided hackers had more luck. One of the hackers monitored by Gargerland stole credit card data, while another tried to steal from a cryptocurrency exchange — although it isn't clear whether they were successful.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday rebuffed a bid from accused Sept. 11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices to revive plea agreements that they reached with military prosecutors before being revoked by the Biden administration.
In an unsigned order, the high court turned away the appeals from Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash of a lower court decision that prevented a military judge from enforcing pretrial agreements they reached with military prosecutors in 2024, which were withdrawn by then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
In rejecting their case, the government's withdrawal of the plea deals remains in place. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in the court's consideration of the appeal.
Mohammed, Hawsawi and bin 'Atash, were captured in 2003 and charged before a military commission with several crimes for their alleged roles in crafting and perpetrating the Sept. 11 attacks, five of which carry the death penalty. In August, the judge overseeing their cases set a trial date of June 2028, which depends on the parties meeting certain deadlines and milestones on time.
The prosecutions have been mired in lengthy legal delays over whether evidence extracted during their interrogations could be used in court. The defendants were held at secret CIA prisons, where they were subjected to "enhanced interrogation techniques," or torture, before they were moved to Guantanamo Bay in 2006. They were formally charged in 2008.
In 2023, following the appointment of retired Brigadier General Susan Escallier as the Convening Authority for military commissions, military lawyers began discussing plea deals with the defendants. Agreements were subsequently reached in 2024 and approved by Escallier, who oversees the military court at Guantanamo Bay.
Under the terms of the deals, the defendants would plead guilty to all charges arising from their alleged roles in the 9/11 terror attacks and serve life sentences, avoiding the death penalty. But shortly after the agreements were announced, Austin said he was revoking them .
But a military judge ruled in November 2024 that Austin's nullification of the deals was unlawful, rendering the agreements valid and enforceable. A military appeals court then said Austin couldn't rescind the plea deals because the defendants had begun to perform one of the terms.
The Justice Department then asked the D.C. Circuit to step in and find that Austin validly withdrew from the pretrial agreements. The D.C. Circuit sided with the government in a decision last year and ruled that the defense secretary "indisputably" had the authority to withdraw from the plea deals.
"The Secretary acted within the bounds of his legal authority, and we decline to second-guess his judgment," the D.C. Circuit panel found.

articles.title_orig: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.title_zh: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.content_orig:
A California woman who prosecutors allege was spying on a son of Taiwan’s president was indicted this month on charges of conspiracy and being an unregistered foreign agent for China.
The indictment was filed Oct. 9 in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the allegations it lays out mirror an earlier criminal complaint against the woman, Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine.
Prosecutors say Zhang, who also goes by Heather, spied on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his home in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. The spying is alleged to have taken place between roughly June and September 2025, prosecutors claim.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that is the source of 90% of the world’s “leading-edge chip manufacturing,” according to the U.S. International Trade Administration . China claims Taiwan, which the U.S. has no official relationship with , though it is required by law to ensure Taiwan can defend itself.
Prosecutors allege Zhang was under the direction of an unnamed Chinese government official and former classmate at her alma mater, China’s University of International Relations, which is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus,” an FBI investigator said in earlier court documents.
An example of the alleged activity was a request by the former classmate to send him pictures “of the house” where the son lives, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors alleged that Zhang flew from California to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area to conduct surveillance of the unidentified son and his home from outside.
The indictment alleges she captured photos, video and license plate information and sent them to the person alleged to be her Chinese handler. An unidentified person, who had fled to China in September, was with her, prosecutors said.
Zhang also traveled to China in August 2025 to meet with a Chinese government official, returned days later and told the official she would most likely be going to where the victim was the following week, according to the indictment.
Her lawyer, Craig Harbaugh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
Previously, Harbaugh, a veteran criminal defense attorney, described Zhang as an upstanding resident of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of Los Angeles, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said in court Oct. 7.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Sunday.
Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry, said this month after Zhang was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport that he was “not familiar” with the situation and that Beijing “opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative.”
U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim ordered Zhang held in pretrial detention after prosecutors argued she poses a flight risk. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons website shows that she remains in custody.
Zhang is scheduled to appear in federal district court Friday for a post-indictment arraignment. She could face up to 15 years in prison.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.title_zh: Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
French officials are exploring introducing curfews as the country reels from its worst rioting in years after protests over education and the cost of living spiraled into a wave of deadly, country-wide violence that has sparked a blame game at home and threatens to spill over into its European neighbors.
Over the weekend, police fired tear gas into crowds and fought running battles with black-clad, hooded rioters who set fires and broke into shops and government buildings, with images showing historic buildings ablaze.
The mood in the country remained tense on Monday, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asking some cities to impose “partial curfews” to protect people, property and businesses. In Marseille, officials banned all gatherings and demonstrations from midday until 8 p.m. local time in anticipation of any more flare-ups, while protestors blocked access to the Louvre Museum in Paris, forcing it to close.
Those measures were introduced after more than 2,000 people were arrested this past weekend, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands. As France begins to count the cost, accusations are mounting that the government failed to adequately anticipate the scale of the crisis, with an election to succeed French President Emmanuel Macron just six months away.
The vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, authorities and political leaders stress – but the level of fighting and destruction , the worst seen in years, has shaken the nation and prompted forceful condemnations from leaders and the public alike.
“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said on Sunday evening. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”
He also promised to hold meetings this week to discuss “concrete proposals” and to listen to protesters’ demands. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to stem the protests in France – as well as similar demonstrations against costs of living now spreading in other countries nearby.
It started in September with a strike by students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs, who demanded more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.
Students around the country, long frustrated with an understaffed and overcrowded education system, launched protests that at times turned violent. A heavy-handed police response fueled public anger and pushed hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets, especially after videos of a police officer using a banned headlock on a girl.
Within a few weeks, the protests swelled to become a broader movement beyond students, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.
“This can’t go on,” said 57-year-old Maria Pallas, a member of a major French trade union, speaking to CNN at Saturday’s protest in Paris. “There’s the cost of living. There’s unemployment. There’s a bunch of things. A young person will go looking for work, we’ll promise him a lot, and he’ll end up with nothing.”
Over half a million people demonstrated across France on Saturday. For the most part, things were peaceful; far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the crowd in Paris as “moving calmly.”
But in several locations the protests spilled into violence, especially as night fell. In Paris, groups of masked young people looted shops and started fires; in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office; in the central city of Limoges, the spire of a 143-year-old town hall collapsed in flames, reviving painful memories for some of the Notre Dame Cathedral fire. Hundreds of businesses were vandalized across the Île-de-France region, which includes Paris, a local business representative told BFMTV.
The protests subsided somewhat on Sunday, with small pockets flaring, and police firing tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, one of the largest public squares in Paris.
By the end of the weekend, Paris looked like a “war zone,” one visitor to the city told Reuters. Residents across the capital were stunned, with some condemning the looters and rioters, and others placing blame with authorities who failed to address the crisis earlier.
“It’s heartbreaking, heartbreaking seeing our city like this,” said 59-year-old Marseille resident Farida, who did not give a last name, according to Reuters. “If every protest ends with all the shop windows smashed and stores trashed, this simply cannot go on — it cannot go on.”
One Paris resident, 56-year-old Paola Formenti, voiced support for the protesters’ “legitimate” anger, even as she condemned the violence.
In his Sunday address, Macron acknowledged protesters’ grievances and said he would take “a number of international initiatives” to tackle fuel prices and ensure a stable supply from Gulf nations. He did not make any concrete assurances or give further specifics.
Even interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted authorities had failed to anticipate the scale of the riots and offered his resignation, though Macron refused to accept it.
The protests and fallout could shape France’s upcoming election next spring. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed this weekend that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Mélenchon, has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.
Protesters have taken to the streets elsewhere in Europe this weekend, too.
In Belgium, students demonstrated against the state of their education system. In Lisbon, Portugal, tens of thousands of people marched on Saturday to protest rising costs of living and the country’s housing crisis.
In Italy, Milan also saw two consecutive nights of unrest this weekend. Protesters threw stones and looted supermarkets, while police responded with tear gas, and water cannons, and arrested 32 people.
Meanwhile in Albania, students have been taking to the streets for months, protesting perceived government corruption. Demonstrations in the capital Tirana turned violent this weekend, with one person photographed throwing a Molotov cocktail at riot police.
Authorities in many of these countries have condemned the violence and called for calm. The protests have caught the attention of the White House, with Vice President JD Vance posting a video of the burning Limoges town hall on X and blaming the unrest on failed immigration policy.
US President Donald Trump also mentioned the protests during a rally in Georgia this weekend, joking: “Let’s go to France and join the revolution and spend our $5,000 there,” referring to the dividend promised if the Republicans win the midterm elections.
CNN’s Joseph Ataman, Niamh Kennedy, Lisa Courbebaisse, Lucie Lepellec, Catherine Nicholls, Sana Noor Haq, James Legge, Sharon Braithwaite, and Melissa Bell contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China Lectures Israel on the West Bank: What About Tibet?
articles.title_zh: China Lectures Israel on the West Bank: What About Tibet?
articles.content_orig:
Mike Huckabee calls for arrest and prosecution of those responsible as Heidi Levine, 63, recovers in hospital in Israel
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left the Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.
Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, was set upon last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupied West Bank towns.
The photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground,” Levine said. “Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me.” She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
Huckabee, a rightwing ally of President Donald Trump with a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine. In a post on X on Saturday, he noted that she was a US citizen who had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”
Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu , has been ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.
In an interview with the Associated Press on Sunday, Levine said she had been “shocked and insulted” to hear that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as “alleged”, adding that the prime minister “had all the evidence on the table”.
But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, and in a letter signed by several of the country’s top former security and intelligence officials, in which they all expressed shame over the attack.
Levine blamed “Jewish terrorists” for Thursday’s attack and added: “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today.”
The photojournalist also said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries. “I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this,” she said. “They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
The attack on the Palestinian farmers and Levine was followed on Saturday by another outbreak of settler violence directed against European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of the French city of Cambrai, who were visiting the occupied West Bank .
Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground. A masked militant shouted “Vive la France!” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Baudoux told Agence France-Presse after he was attacked. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening. For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.”
Violence is surging ahead of bitterly fought elections to be held on 27 October, with Palestinians’ annual olive harvest being repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement rightwing base.
France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has called on Israel to “urgently halt criminal violence” and to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux. The EU has condemned the attack and urged “full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists”.
The European Commission executive vice-president, Teresa Ribera, went further, posting an interview with Levine in hospital and adding the caption: “They want no witnesses.”
Israel’s foreign ministry has condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
On Monday, Israeli ⁠police said they have ⁠arrested ⁠eight ​suspects as part of an investigation ⁠into violent incidents in the West ⁠Bank over the weekend. The police did not identify the suspects.
Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, called Levine in hospital on Saturday, saying the attack was “outrageous and shocking” and was weighing on his conscience.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the elections, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, criticised the prime minister over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses”. He described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in a post on his Truth Social network on Sunday, hailing him as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He added: “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
The Washington Post has reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation into the attack on Levine, even though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.
Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says about 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Computational analysis ‘solves’ what Mario 64’s infamous plaque says, and it’s not ‘L is Real 2401’
articles.title_zh: Computational analysis ‘solves’ what Mario 64’s infamous plaque says, and it’s not ‘L is Real 2401’
articles.content_orig:
A Super Mario 64 fan has performed an open-source computational analysis in an attempt to finally solve the game’s infamous ‘L is Real 2401’ mystery.
For around 30 years, players have tried to figure out what the plaque on the fountain in Peach’s Castle says in the 1996 Nintendo 64 launch game.
An early theory was that the plaque reads, ‘L is Real 2401’, a potential hint that Luigi might be playable in the game and that 2401 might be a clue on how to unlock him.
In 1996, IGN.com offered $100 to anyone who could figure out how to unlock Luigi, while in its April 1998 issue, Nintendo Power magazine mentioned the ‘L is Real 2401’ theory in an April Fool’s Day feature.
Modern re-releases of the game featuring sharper visuals haven’t made the answer any clearer, since the original plaque text was only written on a small 32×32 pixel tile.
Now programmer Mochi64 has performed a complex analysis on the plaque in an attempt to finally decode what it says, and made their results open-source for others to check.
According to Mochi64, because the two lines of text are 3-5 pixels tall, they’re too small to read, so any attempt to upscale the image is pointless because it’s just guesswork.
Instead, their process used millions of calculations to figure out what combination of words, font, and resizing technique that would have been performed by an artist in the mid-90s would have resulted in pixels closest to those in the plaque.
Using this process, Mochi64 believes the message actually reads ‘Eternal Star’ on the top line, and ‘We Hope So’ on the bottom line, because this provided the closest possible match after millions of comparisons.
Mochi64 applied a scoring system to their tool, which grades each word and phrase on how close a match it is to the original texture. After trying more than 1.2 million words, the above received the lowest (and therefore best) mismatch score of 1,129. By comparison, ‘L is Real 2401’ had a mismatch score of 2,031 on the first line alone.
Mochi64 has also posted a ‘plaque challenge’, where people can use the same open-source code to test another phrase and see if they can get an even lower score, but after their fairly exhaustive process they’re sure this is the definitive answer. As for what it actually means, Nintendo seems unlikely to ever confirm.
Luigi was originally intended as a second playable character in Super Mario 64, according to a 1996 interview with director Shigeru Miyamoto , which is what sparked fascination with the game’s blurry sign.
Speaking via an official strategy guide, Miyamoto described “a room made of simple Lego-like blocks” in which “Mario and Luigi could run around in there, climb slopes, jump around, etc”. This seems to match YouTube footage from a 1995 expo appearing to show the two characters together.
According to Miyamoto, Luigi stayed in Super Mario 64 until the final year of development, after which they removed him due to memory issues.
“We were going to include him in a Mario Bros. style minigame, but because most users probably only have that one controller when they first buy their N64, for that reason (and others) we decided not to,” Miyamoto said at the time.
We finally have a glimpse of what the early multiplayer mode for Super Mario 64 looked like! This is also the first time we have seen Luigi's SM64 model outside of the Nintendo Leaks! Take a look! pic.twitter.com/Ev3R7NDBtp
“I think it would have been great if we’d been able to make it two-player, with Mario and Luigi. But if we had done it wrong, it would have turned into a fighting game or something (laughs), so we’re leaving that challenge for next time.”
In a 2009 Iwata Asks interview , Miyamoto commented again on the canned Mario 64 multiplayer mode, saying: “The screen was split and they went into the castle separately. When they meet in the corridor, I was incredibly happy! (laughs) Then there was also the mode where the camera is fixed and we see Mario running away, steadily getting smaller and smaller.”
If authentic, the Space World 1995 footage is the first documented time Luigi has been seen in the classic N64 game, outside of a high-profile 2020 leak of classic Nintendo game files , which included a model for the character.

articles.title_zh: US threatens Europe with ‘devastating’ retaliation if EU restricts SpaceX’s access to European market
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder told the Financial Times that European companies would face “devastating” retaliation from Washington if Brussels moves forward with plans to restrict American competitors’ access to parts of the European market.
The dispute centers on a European Commission proposal to reserve part of the radio spectrum that lets smartphones connect directly to satellites for European companies, a move that would restrict spectrum access for Chinese and American companies, including SpaceX.
Asked whether European companies should fear retaliation, Puzder said they “should be wary that it could happen and it would be very devastating for those companies,” given the size of the American market.
Puzder said that if the goal “is to make United States less competitive, I think that that’s not a legitimate goal of this kind of legislation.” “You don’t make European companies more competitive by making US companies less competitive,” he added.
SpaceX has sharply criticized the European Commission’s proposal, warning that the move risks degrading communications quality in Ukraine, where Starlink plays a critical role.
On October 14, Ukrainian military officials reported restrictions affecting the operation of Starlink satellite communication terminals, or more precisely, their military version, Starshield. The restrictions emerged amid growing tension between Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump, who, however, claims he did not order the terminals’ operation restricted. The Telegraph’s sources said that SpaceX head Elon Musk proposed restricting Starlink’s operation in Ukraine to Trump, and the U.S. president agreed.

articles.title_orig: French Government-Bond Yields Rise on Protests, Budget Concerns; Treasury Yields Fall
articles.title_zh: French Government-Bond Yields Rise on Protests, Budget Concerns; Treasury Yields Fall
articles.content_orig:
France's parliament begins debate on the 2027 budget Tuesday as high deficits, rising debt and student protests sharpen the political cost of fiscal consolidation.
The euro zone's second-biggest economy is barreling toward a debt crisis, and risks dragging the continent down with it, unless it sustainably brings down its national deficit, according to many market watchers.
Even as thousands take to the streets to protest years of underfunding in public services, particularly education, France has run one of Europe's highest deficit-to-GDP ratios for nearly a decade under President Emmanuel Macron.
Government spending remains well above its peers in the politically sensitive realm of social protections, particularly pensions and healthcare, while tepid economic growth has failed to compensate.
With presidential elections looming next year and parliamentarians proving reluctant to compromise, France's economic and political uncertainty is weighing on the euro .
French government borrowing costs have soared to their highest level in nearly a quarter of a century as jittery bond markets have responded to the country's failure to impose fiscal consolidation.
The widening gap in French bond yields over their German equivalents has raised questions over whether the European Central Bank would have to take the expensive and politically controversial step of intervening to stabilize the market. While this could halt a panic that fragments the currency union, the legacy of the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which hammered countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy — means it would require drastic action from France.
"The ECB will not step in just to 'bail out' France. If there was a European crisis they will intervene in some form but they will not save a country that cannot save itself," Antonio Fatas, professor of Economics at INSEAD Business School, said by email.
